h1: What the CLARITY Act actually does
title: What Is the CLARITY Act? Crypto Market Structure Explained
description: The CLARITY Act splits crypto oversight between the SEC and CFTC using a maturity test. Here is what the bill does, in plain language, with sources.
question: What is the CLARITY Act and what would it change?
tldr: H.R. 3633 draws a line between digital commodities and digital securities, hands the commodity side to the CFTC, and leaves the securities side with the SEC. The line is drawn by a maturity test rather than by asset type.

sections.h2: The problem it was written to solve
body: For a decade, the question of whether a token is a security has been answered one enforcement action at a time. The SEC applied the Howey test case by case. The CFTC claimed bitcoin and ether as commodities. Nobody wrote down a rule that told a builder in advance which regulator they answered to.

The CLARITY Act writes that rule down. It is the first market structure framework to pass a chamber of Congress, and it does something the earlier attempts avoided. It stops arguing about whether a token is a security and starts asking whether the network underneath it is finished.

sections.h2: The maturity test, not the asset test
body: The bill's central move is to look past the token and at the blockchain. A system counts as mature when four things are true at once. It works, meaning you can transact, access services, or take part in validation or governance. It runs on open-source code. It operates under pre-established, transparent rules. And no single person or affiliated group controls it, where holding 20 percent or more of the tokens counts as control.

Pass that test and the asset is a digital commodity, regulated by the CFTC. Fail it and you stay under SEC jurisdiction. The test is about the network's independence from its founders, which is a better proxy for investor risk than asking whether the word 'token' appeared in a pitch deck.
Early Thunder ran the 20 percent control threshold against our own 251-token scorecard. The result is uncomfortable for most of the market, and we published the full distribution.

sections.h2: The ancillary asset carve-out
body: There is a second definition doing quiet work. An ancillary asset is an intangible, commercially fungible asset distributed alongside the sale of a security through an investment contract.

Read that twice. It means the fundraising can have been a securities offering while the token itself trades as something else. The contract was the security. The token was attached to it. That separation is what lets a 2021 seed round with a SAFT survive contact with the new framework instead of tainting the asset forever.

sections.h2: What changes for an ordinary holder
body: Three practical things. Exchanges get a registration path that does not require them to guess which of their listings is a security, which is why delistings have been the default risk-management move since 2023. Banks and brokerages get a rulebook they can hand to a compliance committee, which is the actual gate on institutional distribution. And issuers get disclosure obligations that scale with maturity rather than a binary registered-or-illegal choice.
What it does not do is make any token a good investment. A clean classification says the venue is legal. It says nothing about whether the protocol earns anything.

faqs.question: Is the CLARITY Act law?
faqs.answer: No. It passed the House 294-134 on July 17 2025 and cleared the Senate Banking Committee 15-9 on May 14 2026. It sits on the Senate Legislative Calendar as Calendar No. 423 with no floor vote scheduled and no cloture motion filed.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the CLARITY Act and the GENIUS Act?
faqs.answer: The GENIUS Act governs stablecoin issuance, reserves, and redemption. The CLARITY Act governs everything else, meaning which regulator oversees trading, custody, and disclosure for non-stablecoin digital assets. They are separate bills solving separate problems.

faqs.question: Who wrote the CLARITY Act?
faqs.answer: Rep. French Hill (R-AR), chairman of the House Financial Services Committee, introduced H.R. 3633 on May 29 2025. The Senate rewrite has been led by Senator Tim Scott, Senator Cynthia Lummis, and Senator Bernie Moreno.

faqs.question: Does the CLARITY Act cover DeFi and self-custody?
faqs.answer: Partly. Section 10307 of the Senate text mentions self-hosted wallets under a financial inclusion heading inside the anti-terrorism framework. That is an acknowledgement rather than the affirmative safe harbour self-custody advocates asked for, and it remains one of the live disputes.

h1: Where the CLARITY Act stands right now
title: CLARITY Act Status and Timeline, July 2026
description: Every dated milestone from introduction to the 600-page Senate text, with the vote counts and what still has to happen before the bill becomes law.
question: Has the CLARITY Act passed, and what is the current status?
tldr: Passed the House. Cleared Senate Banking. On the calendar since June 1 2026 with no floor vote scheduled. Needs 60 Senate votes and a merge with a separate Agriculture Committee bill before it can reach the President.

sections.h2: Three gates, one cleared and a half
body: A bill becomes law by passing both chambers in identical form. The CLARITY Act has cleared one chamber and one committee of the second. That sounds close. It is not, because the hard part in the Senate has never been the committee.

The House vote on July 17 2025 was 294-134, with every voting Republican and 78 Democrats in favour. That margin matters as a signal. It means the concept has bipartisan support when the text is not carrying a fight about the current administration.
The Senate Banking Committee vote on May 14 2026 was 15-9. Two Democrats crossed over, and both said plainly that a committee vote did not commit them on the floor.

sections.h2: What being on the calendar does and does not mean
body: The bill became Calendar No. 423 on June 1 2026. Placement on the Senate Legislative Calendar means the bill is eligible for floor consideration. It does not schedule anything.

The step that actually matters is a cloture motion, which is how the majority leader forces a vote on proceeding. None has been filed. Until one is, the count of supportive senators is a poll, not a whip count.

sections.h2: The second bill nobody talks about
body: Senate Agriculture has its own vehicle, S. 3755, the Digital Commodity Intermediaries Act. Because the CLARITY framework gives the CFTC the commodity side, and the CFTC answers to the Agriculture committees, the Banking text and the Agriculture text have to be reconciled before either moves.
That is a second negotiation stacked on top of the first, between two committees that do not have to agree. It is the least covered obstacle and one of the more durable ones.

sections.h2: The July 2026 text
body: Senators Lummis and Moreno released the full 600-page Senate text on July 24 2026, two days after announcing negotiated ethics language with the White House. Seven Democratic senators said the same day that the bill falls short on ethics for elected officials, consumer protection, and illicit finance.
Lummis framed the stakes without hedging. The coming weeks, she said, are likely the last real chance we will have for years to get this right.

faqs.question: When will the Senate vote on the CLARITY Act?
faqs.answer: No vote is scheduled. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said on July 23 2026 that he would like to at least get Clarity started and that they will see where the votes are. White House crypto adviser Patrick Witt pointed to the first week of August as a possible window.

faqs.question: How many votes does the CLARITY Act need in the Senate?
faqs.answer: Sixty, to overcome a filibuster. With a Republican majority, that means seven to nine Democratic votes depending on the exact caucus count and attendance.

faqs.question: What happens if the CLARITY Act does not pass in 2026?
faqs.answer: The bill dies with the 119th Congress and has to be reintroduced from scratch in the next one. Midterm elections on November 3 2026 mean the reintroduced bill would face a Senate with a different composition and different committee leadership.

h1: Why the CLARITY Act is stuck
title: Why the CLARITY Act Is Stalled in the Senate
description: Four disputes are blocking the CLARITY Act, and only one is about market structure. Ethics language, stablecoin yield, AML reporting, and a committee turf fight.
keywords: why is the clarity act stalled
question: Why has the CLARITY Act not passed the Senate?
tldr: Four separate fights, and the loudest one has nothing to do with crypto market structure. Ethics language about elected officials is doing more to hold up the bill than any disagreement about the SEC and CFTC.

sections.h2: The ethics fight is not a market structure fight
body: The provision restricting elected officials and their families from issuing or promoting digital assets is the reason the bill has not moved. Sponsors negotiated language with the White House and announced it on July 22 2026. Democrats called it insufficient within 48 hours, and seven of them put that in writing on July 24.

Worth separating out, because it means the bill's fate is only partly a function of crypto policy. A framework that both parties largely agree on is being held hostage to a dispute about the conduct of one administration. That has two consequences. It makes the odds harder to model from policy fundamentals. And it means a change in political circumstance could move the bill faster than any amount of industry lobbying.

sections.h2: Banks versus crypto on stablecoin yield
body: The banking lobby argued that letting stablecoin issuers pay yield to holders would pull deposits out of community banks and into tokenised dollars. A bipartisan group added limits.

Coinbase walked. Brian Armstrong pulled the company's support in January 2026, and the markup slipped. Stablecoins were close to 20 percent of Coinbase revenue at $355M in Q3 2025, so the objection was not abstract.

The split runs through Wall Street too. Goldman's David Solomon says he is very supportive of moving the Clarity Act forward. JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon and the Bank Policy Institute are on the other side of the yield question. When the two largest US banks disagree in public about a provision, that provision does not get quietly dropped.

sections.h2: Illicit finance and the self-custody question
body: Law enforcement groups and several Banking Democrats want stronger reporting obligations on intermediaries before they supply floor votes. The Senate text handles self-hosted wallets in Section 10307, under a financial inclusion heading inside the anti-terrorism framework.

That placement tells you the drafters knew they had to say something about self-custody and had not agreed what. It acknowledges the practice without protecting it. Neither side is satisfied, which is usually a sign the language will be rewritten again.

sections.h2: Two committees, one CFTC
body: Senate Agriculture oversees the CFTC and has its own bill, S. 3755. Since the CLARITY framework hands the commodity side of the market to the CFTC, Agriculture has a legitimate claim on the text and no obligation to defer to Banking.
Merging the two is a negotiation between committees, not between parties. It generates no headlines and it has to finish before floor time is worth requesting.

faqs.question: Which senators are blocking the CLARITY Act?
faqs.answer: Seven Democratic senators stated on July 24 2026 that the bill falls short on ethics for elected officials, consumer protection, and illicit finance. The two Democrats who voted for it in committee on May 14 both said their committee votes did not commit them on the floor.

faqs.question: Why did Coinbase withdraw support for the CLARITY Act?
faqs.answer: In January 2026, over Senate language limiting yield paid to stablecoin holders. Coinbase argued the stablecoin and banking provisions would let large banks restrict competition and reduce incentives for crypto-native payment products.

faqs.question: Is the CLARITY Act dead?
faqs.answer: No, but the 2026 window is narrow. The bill remains on the Senate calendar. The realistic paths are a floor vote in the first week of August or in the short September session before the chamber leaves to campaign.

h1: Who is backing the CLARITY Act, and what their numbers really mean
title: Who Supports the CLARITY Act? The $30 Trillion Claim, Checked
description: BlackRock, Schwab, Fidelity and Goldman back the bill. The widely quoted $30 trillion figure adds together three different kinds of assets. Here is the breakdown.
question: Which institutions support the CLARITY Act and how much money do they actually control?
tldr: The headline number circulating is that firms with more than $30 trillion back the bill. The four largest backers report $39.6 trillion between them, but only about $22 trillion of that is discretionary. The rest is custody and supervision, which is a different thing.

sections.h2: The number everybody is quoting
body: Coverage of the July 2026 push settled on a figure. Firms controlling north of $30 trillion have lined up behind the bill, with some estimates closer to $50 trillion depending on how you count. That parenthetical is doing an enormous amount of work, and almost nobody follows it up.
So we did. Four firms carry most of the weight, and each reports a different kind of number.

sections.h2: Three accounting categories, added together
body: BlackRock reported $15.34 trillion in assets under management at June 30 2026, a record, up from $12.53 trillion a year earlier on $192 billion of quarterly net inflows. That is discretionary. BlackRock decides where it goes.

Charles Schwab reported $13.08 trillion in total client assets for the same quarter. That is custody. The money belongs to Schwab's clients and Schwab does not allocate it. Adding it to BlackRock's AUM as though both represent capital that can be pointed at an asset class is a category error.

Fidelity's figure moves depending on the article. The $7.1 trillion number is discretionary managed assets as of the end of 2025. The $18 trillion number is everything Fidelity administers. Both appear in coverage, usually without a label.

Goldman Sachs reported $4.041 trillion in assets under supervision at June 30 2026, a record after $91 billion of long-term net inflows. Assets under supervision is broader than AUM and includes advisory relationships Goldman does not direct.

Add the headline figures and you get $39.6 trillion. Add only the discretionary pools and you get roughly $22.4 trillion. Neither is the number of dollars that would move into digital assets if the bill passed, and that is the point.

sections.h2: The one disclosure worth more than all of it
body: Schwab's useful contribution is not its balance sheet. It is a share figure. Schwab has said its clients already hold roughly 20 percent of all US crypto ETP assets.

Apply that to the market. US spot bitcoin ETPs held about $80 billion and spot ether ETPs $10.48 billion around July 21 2026. A fifth of that is roughly $18 billion to $19 billion of crypto ETP exposure sitting in Schwab accounts already, before any legislation passes. Treat it as an order of magnitude, since ETP assets move with price.

That number tells you something the trillions do not. Retail and advised money reached crypto through the ETP wrapper without waiting for market structure legislation. The constraint that CLARITY would remove is not appetite. It is the set of products a compliance committee will approve, which is a narrower and more specific thing than $30 trillion of firepower.

sections.h2: Why they want it anyway
body: Schwab called the bill a really important fundamental catalyst that needs to pass, and launched crypto trading this year. Fidelity said the time is now for clear rules of the road. Goldman's CEO said he is very supportive of moving it forward while conceding the bill is not perfect.

Read those together and the motivation is consistent. None of these firms is asking for permission to buy tokens. They are asking for a rulebook that lets them build products, custody assets, and answer a regulator's question without hiring outside counsel first. Rules reduce legal cost. That is the trade, and it is a smaller and more believable claim than a $30 trillion wall of money.

faqs.question: Does BlackRock support the CLARITY Act?
faqs.answer: Yes. BlackRock is named among the financial firms backing the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act alongside Goldman Sachs, Fidelity, Charles Schwab, and Grayscale.

faqs.question: How much are Schwab clients holding in crypto ETPs?
faqs.answer: Schwab has said its clients hold roughly 20 percent of all US crypto ETP assets. Against US spot bitcoin ETP assets of about $80 billion and ether ETP assets of $10.48 billion as of July 21 2026, that implies roughly $18 billion to $19 billion. Early Thunder derived that figure, Schwab did not disclose it, and it moves with price.

faqs.question: Is the $30 trillion supporting the CLARITY Act real money for crypto?
faqs.answer: No. The figure aggregates discretionary assets under management, custodial client assets, and assets under supervision, which are three different things. Only the discretionary portion represents capital the firms themselves allocate, and none of it is earmarked for digital assets.

h1: How the CLARITY Act divides the SEC and the CFTC
title: SEC vs CFTC Crypto Jurisdiction Under the CLARITY Act
description: The bill sends digital commodities to the CFTC and digital securities to the SEC. What decides which side an asset lands on, and what each regulator gets.
question: Under the CLARITY Act, does the SEC or the CFTC regulate a given crypto asset?
tldr: The CFTC gets spot market oversight of digital commodities, which is new authority it has asked for repeatedly. The SEC keeps assets whose networks have not reached maturity, plus the fundraising contracts that created them.

sections.h2: What each regulator ends up holding
body: The CFTC gets registration, trading, and market conduct for digital commodities, meaning assets tied to a mature blockchain system. That authority is genuinely new. The CFTC has had derivatives authority over bitcoin futures for years while having no direct writ over the spot market, a gap it has complained about since 2018.

The SEC keeps assets that fail the maturity test and keeps the investment contracts through which tokens were originally sold. It also keeps disclosure obligations for issuers, which is where most ongoing compliance cost lives.

sections.h2: The line is drawn once, not permanently
body: The design that separates this bill from earlier attempts is that classification can change. A network that is founder-controlled at launch sits under the SEC. If it decentralises to the point of passing the maturity test, the asset moves.

That is a better model than the alternatives, and it creates a specific incentive. Distributing supply and giving up control now has a regulatory payoff, not just a rhetorical one. Whether teams will actually give up 20 percent-plus positions to get it is an open question, and the current supply distribution across the market suggests most have not started.

sections.h2: Why two committees make this harder
body: The CFTC answers to the Agriculture committees, not Banking. So a bill written in Senate Banking that hands new authority to the CFTC needs Senate Agriculture to agree, and Agriculture has its own bill, S. 3755, the Digital Commodity Intermediaries Act.
Any final text is a merge of the two. That is why the jurisdictional split, which sounds like the settled part of the bill, is still an active negotiation.

sections.h2: What it means for exchanges
body: Today a US exchange listing a token carries the risk that the SEC later calls it an unregistered security. The rational response has been to delist anything ambiguous, which is why the US listed universe is narrower than the global one.

With a written test, that risk becomes assessable in advance. An exchange can run the maturity test, document the conclusion, and register with the appropriate regulator. It does not remove judgement calls at the margin. It moves them from after the fact to before.

faqs.question: Would bitcoin be regulated by the CFTC under the CLARITY Act?
faqs.answer: Bitcoin comfortably satisfies the mature blockchain system criteria as written. It is functional, open source, rule-based, and has no entity holding 20 percent or more of supply. That places it on the digital commodity side, under CFTC oversight.

faqs.question: Does the SEC lose power under the CLARITY Act?
faqs.answer: It loses spot market oversight of assets that pass the maturity test. It keeps everything else, including all investment contracts, issuer disclosure, and every asset whose network remains controlled. Given how few tokens clear the control threshold, the practical reduction in SEC reach is smaller than the framing suggests.

faqs.question: Can an asset move from SEC to CFTC oversight over time?
faqs.answer: Yes. That is the design. Classification follows the state of the network, so an asset that decentralises past the control threshold can transition from the securities side to the commodity side.

h1: The mature blockchain system test and the 20 percent rule
title: Mature Blockchain System Test, the CLARITY Act 20% Rule
description: Four conditions decide whether a network is mature under the CLARITY Act. The one that disqualifies most tokens is the 20 percent control threshold.
question: What is a mature blockchain system under the CLARITY Act and what is the 20 percent threshold?
tldr: Four conditions, all required. Functional, open source, rule-based, and not controlled by any person or group. Holding 20 percent or more of tokens counts as control, and that clause does more filtering than the other three combined.

sections.h2: The four conditions
body: A blockchain system qualifies as mature when it is functional for executing transactions, accessing services, or taking part in validation or decentralised governance. It has to be composed of open-source code. It has to operate on pre-established, transparent rules. And it cannot be subject to the control of a single person or group, including by holding 20 percent or more of the tokens.

The first three are close to free. Nearly every serious protocol is functional, open source, and rule-based. Those conditions screen out vapourware, not real projects. The fourth is where the framework actually bites.

sections.h2: Why 20 percent is a harder bar than it sounds
body: Twenty percent is not an unusual founding allocation. It is close to the median one. A typical 2021 to 2023 token launch reserved something like 15 to 25 percent for the team, another 15 to 20 percent for investors, and a further slice for a foundation treasury.

The question that decides classification is whether those buckets get counted together. A foundation, a founding team, and the investors from a single round can plausibly be read as an affiliated group. If they are, the arithmetic disqualifies a large share of the market. If each is assessed separately, far fewer tokens fail. The bill text sets the threshold without resolving the aggregation question, and that ambiguity is doing a lot of unacknowledged work.
Early Thunder ran the concentration question across our 251-token scorecard to see how much of the market sits near the line. The distribution is published in full.

sections.h2: The incentive it creates
body: Read as policy rather than as law, the threshold is a lever. It tells teams that giving up control has a defined payoff, which is CFTC oversight instead of SEC oversight, and with it a workable listing and custody path.

That is a real incentive and it points the right way. The catch is timing. Distributing supply below 20 percent is slow, involves vesting schedules written years ago, and dilutes the people making the decision. Expect announcements about decentralisation to outrun actual changes in supply distribution by a wide margin.

sections.h2: What it does not measure
body: The test says nothing about whether governance is meaningful, whether a multisig can pause the chain, or whether validator sets are concentrated. A protocol could distribute tokens broadly while five entities run the sequencers.

So treat the maturity test as a supply-distribution screen with a decentralisation label on it. It is a defensible place to draw a legal line because supply is measurable. It is not the same as being decentralised, and it would be a mistake to read a passing grade as one.

faqs.question: What counts as control under the CLARITY Act?
faqs.answer: Control includes holding 20 percent or more of a network's tokens, along with the general condition that the system is not subject to the control of a single person or group. The bill sets the numeric threshold without fully settling how affiliated holders are aggregated.

faqs.question: Which tokens pass the mature blockchain system test?
faqs.answer: Bitcoin and Ethereum clear it comfortably on every published criterion. Beyond those, it depends heavily on how team, foundation, and investor allocations are aggregated. Early Thunder's scan of 251 tokens found that 194 of them score in the lower half of our holder concentration measure.

faqs.question: Does a token have to be fully decentralised to be a digital commodity?
faqs.answer: No. The test is specific and narrower than decentralisation in the general sense. A network can pass on supply distribution while remaining concentrated in validators, sequencers, or governance participation.

h1: Which tokens are exposed if the CLARITY Act passes
title: CLARITY Act Token Classification Risk, 251 Tokens Scored
description: We scored 251 tokens against the CLARITY Act's control and regulatory tests. Only six clear the top band, and $138B of market cap sits in the most exposed one.
question: Which crypto assets are most exposed to classification risk under the CLARITY Act?
tldr: Six of 251 tokens score in our top readiness band. Median score is 45 out of 100. Excluding bitcoin and ether, 32 percent of tracked altcoin market cap sits in the most exposed band, and BNB and TRON alone account for most of it.

sections.h2: What we measured and how
body: Early Thunder maintains a 251-token scorecard rating each asset across 25 variables from 1 to 10. Three of those variables map directly onto what the CLARITY Act cares about. Regulatory safety captures existing enforcement exposure and jurisdictional posture. Holder concentration captures how much supply sits with insiders, which is the variable that speaks to the 20 percent control threshold. Institutional adoption captures whether regulated venues already touch the asset.

We combined them into a readiness score out of 100, weighting regulatory safety at 50 percent, holder concentration at 30 percent, and institutional adoption at 20 percent. Regulatory safety carries the most weight because it reflects the position an asset is already in. Concentration comes second because it is the mechanical test. Treat it as our own heuristic, derived from our own research. It is not a legal opinion and not a prediction of any regulator's decision.

sections.h2: The distribution is worse than the narrative
body: Six tokens out of 251 score 70 or above. Ethereum leads at 88, bitcoin at 83, then Avalanche, Chainlink, Uniswap, and Maker. Seventy-three tokens land between 50 and 69. One hundred and fifty-three sit between 35 and 49. Nineteen fall below 35.

The median is 45 out of 100. That is the headline. The market talks about the CLARITY Act as a rising tide, and for the assets already on the right side of the line it probably is. For the median token in a broad altcoin portfolio, a written classification test is not obviously good news. It converts an unresolved question into a documented answer, and the answer is not guaranteed to be favourable.

The concentration numbers explain most of it. Of 251 tokens, 194 score four or below on holder concentration, and 55 score three or below. Insider-heavy supply is the norm, not the exception, and it is the exact characteristic the 20 percent control threshold is written to catch.

sections.h2: Where the money actually sits
body: Aggregate market cap tells a sharper story than token counts. The top band holds $1.74 trillion, but that is bitcoin and ether doing nearly all the work. Strip those two out and the picture inverts.

Of the $429 billion of remaining tracked market cap, $138 billion sits in the most exposed band. That is 32 percent. Two names carry most of it. BNB scores 29 against $88.7 billion of market cap, and TRON scores 25 against $35.5 billion. Both are penalised on the same two axes, low regulatory safety and concentrated supply, and both are large enough that their treatment would move the market's sense of what the framework means in practice.

The rest of the exposed band is a mix of privacy assets, exchange tokens, and gaming or meme names. Monero at 29 is a category of its own, since the issue there is not supply distribution but whether a privacy-preserving asset fits any of the bill's boxes.

sections.h2: How to use this
body: Not as a buy or sell list. Classification readiness is one input, and it says nothing about whether a protocol earns money or has users. A high readiness score on an asset with no revenue is still an asset with no revenue.

What it is good for is sizing an unhedged exposure. If a portfolio is concentrated in names from the bottom band, then a bill passing is a risk event rather than a catalyst, and that is the opposite of the position most holders think they are in. Reading the score alongside a protocol's actual revenue is the more useful exercise, and both live on the same scorecard.

faqs.question: Which tokens score best on CLARITY Act readiness?
faqs.answer: Ethereum at 88 and bitcoin at 83 lead, followed by Avalanche at 78, Chainlink at 77, Uniswap at 76, and Maker at 71. Those six are the only assets of 251 scoring 70 or above on Early Thunder's readiness composite.

faqs.question: Which large-cap tokens are most exposed to classification risk?
faqs.answer: By market cap in the lowest band, BNB at $88.7 billion scores 29, TRON at $35.5 billion scores 25, and Monero at $7.0 billion scores 29. Together the lowest band holds $138 billion, which is 32 percent of tracked market cap excluding bitcoin and ether.

faqs.question: Is a low readiness score a prediction that a token will be ruled a security?
faqs.answer: No. It is Early Thunder's own composite of three research variables that map onto what the bill measures. Regulators, courts, and the final text will decide actual classifications, and the bill is not law.

faqs.question: How many tokens fail the concentration test?
faqs.answer: Of the 251 tokens scored, 194 sit at four or below on our holder concentration measure and 55 sit at three or below. Concentrated insider supply is the market norm, and it is the characteristic the 20 percent control threshold targets.

h1: The floor-time arithmetic behind CLARITY Act passage
title: Will the CLARITY Act Pass in 2026? The Calendar Math
description: Passage does not hinge on support, it hinges on floor days. Counting the Senate's remaining 2026 session time shows how narrow the window really is.
question: What are the odds the CLARITY Act passes in 2026?
tldr: Two windows remain. The first week of August, and a short stretch after the Senate returns on September 14. October is gone to campaigning and Election Day is November 3. Support is not the binding constraint. Floor time is.

sections.h2: Count the days, not the endorsements
body: Most coverage measures momentum in endorsements. A better measure is how many days the Senate is physically in session with floor time available for a bill that is not must-pass.

The chamber sits for the first week of August and then leaves. It returns on September 14. Senators are then scheduled out of Washington for nearly all of October and the first week of November, with Election Day on November 3. That leaves two windows, and the second is competing with appropriations, nominations, and every other item that accumulated over a five-week recess.
A market structure bill is not must-pass. It has no funding cliff and no expiring authority forcing action. Bills without a deadline lose to bills with one, every time floor time is scarce.

sections.h2: The steps still required
body: Reaching a floor vote is not one step. The Banking text has to be reconciled with Senate Agriculture's S. 3755. A cloture motion has to be filed, which the majority leader will not do without a count. Cloture itself takes floor time, and post-cloture debate takes more. Then, assuming Senate passage, the House and Senate versions have to be reconciled, and the House would need to take up the result.

Each of those consumes days that the calendar does not have. Which is why Senate Majority Leader John Thune said on July 23 that he would like to at least get Clarity started and would see where the votes are. That is the language of a leader managing a queue, not one scheduling a win. White House crypto adviser Patrick Witt said he was perplexed by it and pointed to the first week of August.

sections.h2: What would actually move it
body: One thing. A deal on the ethics language that seven Senate Democrats can sign. Every other dispute in this bill has a technical fix that lobbyists and committee staff can draft. The ethics provision is about the conduct of a sitting administration, which means it is resolved politically or not at all.

That makes the odds unusually reflexive. Industry support, and the $22 trillion of genuinely discretionary capital behind it, does not move a senator whose objection is about presidential conflicts of interest. Watch the ethics negotiation, not the endorsement count.

Lummis put the stakes plainly on July 24. The coming weeks, she said, are likely the last real chance we will have for years to get this right. She is describing the calendar, not being dramatic. A bill that does not pass this Congress starts over in a Senate reshaped by the midterms.

sections.h2: How to position around it
body: Two things follow from the calendar. First, headline risk is asymmetric in the near term. Passage is a real possibility in a narrow window, and failure is the base case simply because the days are not there. Anything priced as though passage is scheduled is priced ahead of the facts.

Second, and less obvious, passage is not uniformly bullish across the market. Our classification work found that 32 percent of tracked altcoin market cap outside bitcoin and ether sits in the most exposed readiness band. For those assets a written test is a resolution risk rather than a catalyst. The tokens with the most to gain are the ones that already had the least classification uncertainty.

faqs.question: When is the last realistic chance for the CLARITY Act in 2026?
faqs.answer: The first week of August, then the September session after the Senate returns on the 14th. The chamber is scheduled out for nearly all of October ahead of the November 3 midterms, which effectively closes the year.

faqs.question: What single factor decides whether the CLARITY Act passes?
faqs.answer: The ethics provision covering elected officials and their families. Every other open dispute has a technical fix available. That one is political, and it is what seven Senate Democrats cited on July 24 2026.

faqs.question: Would the CLARITY Act be bullish for crypto if it passed?
faqs.answer: Not evenly. Assets that already sit on the commodity side of the line gain a clear listing and custody path. Assets with concentrated supply and existing enforcement exposure face a documented answer to a question that is currently unresolved. Early Thunder's scan puts 32 percent of tracked altcoin market cap outside bitcoin and ether in the most exposed band.
